identification.summary: PRC state-sponsored cyber-espionage cluster targeting the core of telecommunications networks: provider-edge and customer-edge routers, network management and authentication infrastructure. Publicly exposed from September 2024 after intrusions into multiple US telecommunications providers, with collection against lawful-intercept systems and the communications of senior US political figures. US agencies and partners describe overlapping commercial designations and state the activity continues worldwide [S1][S2][S4][S5].
identification.firstObserved: Activity under overlapping designations (GhostEmperor, FamousSparrow) publicly reported from 2021 [S9]. Cisco Talos observed persistence in one victim environment for over three years as of February 2025 [S3].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Salt Typhoon. Microsoft maps OPERATOR PANDA, GhostEmperor and FamousSparrow to it [S8]. AA25-239A lists overlapping designations including RedMike, UNC5807 and GhostEmperor [S1]; Trend Micro tracks overlapping activity as Earth Estries. Overlap is not identity: vendors draw cluster boundaries differently.

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China. OFAC designated Sichuan Juxinhe Network Technology Co., Ltd. for 'direct involvement' in Salt Typhoon intrusions and described it as part of a contractor pool used by the Ministry of State Security (MSS) [S2]. AA25-239A names Sichuan Juxinhe, Beijing Huanyu Tianqiong Information Technology Co. and Sichuan Zhixin Ruijie Network Technology Co. as firms providing cyber products and services to PRC intelligence and military units [S1].
attribution.confidence: Formal US government attribution: FBI/CISA joint statement (Nov 2024) [S4], OFAC designation (Jan 2025) [S2], and a multinational joint advisory (Aug 2025) [S1]. The underlying technical attribution evidence has not been published.
attribution.basis: Incident response across US telecommunications victims, vendor forensics (Cisco Talos) [S3], sanctions findings [S2], and the joint advisory's TTP and infrastructure reporting [S1].

objectives: Strategic intelligence collection through telecommunications infrastructure. Reported effects include theft of customer call-record metadata, collection of call and text content from a limited number of individuals in government and political activity, and copying of information subject to US law-enforcement requests under court order [S4]. Joint reporting describes the intent as giving PRC intelligence the ability to identify and track targets' communications and movements worldwide [S1]. Exfiltration of network configuration files supports follow-on intrusions elsewhere [S6].

sectors: Military infrastructure networks, including a US state Army National Guard network (Mar–Dec 2024)
regions: United States (FBI: at least 200 US organizations affected)
Global: organizations in more than 80 countries (FBI, Aug 2025)
targeting.notes: Sector list as reported from AA25-239A coverage [S1][S5]. National Guard compromise from a DHS I&A memo dated 11 Jun 2025, reported Jul 2025 [S6]. The Singapore telecommunications intrusions disclosed in 2025–2026 were attributed by Singapore to UNC3886, not Salt Typhoon [S10].

capabilities.summary: Credential-led access to network infrastructure: in nearly all cases Talos investigated, initial access to Cisco devices used legitimate stolen credentials, with one case of likely CVE-2018-0171 (Cisco Smart Install) exploitation [S3]. Post-access, the actor harvests further credentials from device configurations and captured SNMP, TACACS and RADIUS traffic, modifies router configurations, clears logs, and persists across multi-vendor equipment for years [S3]. Custom tooling includes JumbledPath, a Go-based ELF that runs packet capture on Cisco devices through actor-defined jump hosts [S3][S7]. Vulnerabilities cited across the broader campaign include Cisco IOS XE CVE-2023-20198/20273, Ivanti CVE-2023-46805/CVE-2024-21887 and Palo Alto CVE-2024-3400 [S1].

campaigns.name: GhostEmperor / FamousSparrow disclosures
campaigns.summary: Kaspersky (GhostEmperor, Demodex rootkit) and ESET (FamousSparrow) report espionage against governments, telecoms and hotels. Microsoft now maps both names to Salt Typhoon.

campaigns.name: FBI/CISA joint statement
campaigns.summary: US government confirms a broad and significant PRC cyber-espionage campaign against commercial telecommunications infrastructure, including call-record theft, collection from individuals in government or political activity, and copying of lawful-intercept request information.

campaigns.name: Army National Guard network compromise
campaigns.summary: DHS I&A memo (11 Jun 2025) reports a US state Army National Guard network was 'extensively compromised', including configuration data and traffic with counterpart networks in every other state and at least four territories. A separate Jan–Mar 2024 theft of state-agency configuration files enabled a later compromise of another government network.

campaigns.name: OFAC sanctions
campaigns.summary: Treasury designates Sichuan Juxinhe Network Technology for direct involvement in Salt Typhoon intrusions against US telecommunications and internet providers.

campaigns.name: Cisco Talos technical findings
campaigns.summary: Credential-led access, one likely CVE-2018-0171 case, JumbledPath packet capture, log clearing, persistence above three years in one environment; no new Cisco vulnerabilities found.

campaigns.name: AA25-239A multinational advisory
campaigns.summary: CISA, NSA, FBI and international partners publish router-focused TTPs and name three PRC contractor firms. FBI states at least 200 US organizations and organizations in more than 80 countries were affected.

diamond.adversary: PRC state-sponsored operators working through contractor firms (Sichuan Juxinhe, Beijing Huanyu Tianqiong, Sichuan Zhixin Ruijie) that serve MSS and PLA customers [S1][S2].
diamond.capability: Stolen valid credentials; n-day edge-device exploits (CVE-2018-0171, CVE-2023-20198/20273, CVE-2023-46805, CVE-2024-21887, CVE-2024-3400); router configuration tampering; SNMP/TACACS/RADIUS capture; JumbledPath; log clearing; Demodex rootkit in earlier overlapping activity [S1][S3][S9].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised network devices used as relays, including pivots from one telecommunications provider's device to another's; actor-controlled jump-host chains for packet-capture tasking and exfiltration [S3].
diamond.victim: Telecommunications backbone and edge, lawful-intercept systems, government, military (state Army National Guard), transportation and lodging networks across the US and 80+ countries [S1][S4][S5][S6].
diamond.socioPolitical: Collection on US government and political leadership communications and on US lawful-intercept targeting, serving PRC intelligence requirements [S4].
diamond.technology: Exploits the trust and low monitoring of network infrastructure devices; configuration files double as intelligence and as enablers for the next intrusion [S3][S6].

gaps: Full victim list and current eviction status at US and allied carriers are not public; FBI statements describe the activity as ongoing [S5].
Technical basis for the MSS link has not been published; attribution rests on sanctions findings and joint-advisory judgments [S1][S2].

Cluster boundaries: overlap among Salt Typhoon, Earth Estries, GhostEmperor, FamousSparrow, UNC2286 and UNC5807 is asserted by different vendors on different evidence. Confirm per-designation before merging reporting.
Your imported record cited the Mandiant UNC4841 (Barracuda ESG) blog as a Salt Typhoon reference. UNC4841 is a separate cluster; that reference was dropped from this profile.
Your salt_typhoon_research_brief lists 'Singapore — all four national telecommunications providers' under Salt Typhoon. Singapore attributed that campaign to UNC3886 [S10]. Correct the brief.
AA25-239A primary text could not be fetched from this environment (cisa.gov blocked). The alias list (UNC5807) and CVE list should be checked against the PDF.
Possible relationship between Salt Typhoon's configuration-file theft and Volt Typhoon's pre-positioning is not established in public reporting.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Treat commercial telecommunications backbone, including leased circuits carrying DoD traffic, as part of the cyberspace OE and as assumed-compromised terrain. STEP 2: Communications terrain is not neutral. Adversary collection may be reading metadata and selected content on unencrypted commercial paths, which affects OPSEC, deception and force-protection estimates. STEP 3: The doctrinal template is valid credentials, then router configuration changes, then credential capture from AAA protocols, then packet capture and config exfiltration, with multi-year dwell. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued quiet collection on government and military communications and on lawful-intercept targeting. MDCOA is using collected configurations and credentials to support disruption or to enable another PRC cluster's pre-positioning during a crisis. Candidate indicators: unexpected ACL or loopback changes, new GRE/IPsec tunnels, Guest Shell activation, non-standard SSH ports, and AAA traffic anomalies [S1][S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Assume degraded confidentiality on commercial paths in C2 planning; prioritize end-to-end encryption and authenticated identity for operational traffic. (2) Network-device telemetry such as config diffs, AAA logs and NetFlow is the primary detection layer. JCC2 data integration should ingest it from DODIN and, by agreement, from carrier partners. (3) Authorities: carriers are private critical infrastructure. Response leads are CISA, the FBI and the FCC, with DoD supporting through DISA and service providers. Command relationships should not assume DoD access to carrier networks. (4) Counterintelligence integration: compromise of lawful-intercept systems is a CI equity, so fuse CI reporting into the threat picture used by Cyber Protection Team (CPT) and Mission Defense Team (MDT) planners.
